# Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling

Rui Melo^(1,2) Andre Duarte^(1,\*) Aditya Oke^(1,\*) Shubham Gandhi¹
Nachiket Kotalwar¹ Rui Abreu² Lei Li¹ Carolyn Rose¹ ¹Carnegie Mellon
University ²FEUP

###### Abstract

Security bugs often slip past static analysis not because they are
impossible to detect, but because detection rules have not yet been
written for the code in front of us. New frameworks, APIs, and coding
idioms continually create such gaps, leaving developers to discover
failures and manually encode new rules.

We present SESAA, a framework in which an LLM (LLM) agent starts from no
rules and iteratively evolves a set of readable and auditable Joern
queries. The agent receives feedback only from a second LLM critic,
which inspects flagged and unflagged code to identify likely false
alarms and suspected misses, without access to ground-truth labels. The
agent then uses this feedback to revise its queries.

On the OWASP Benchmark for Python, SESAA reaches a mean $`F_{1}`$ of
$`0.742{}`$ across $`8{}`$ independent runs, well above the default
configurations of five widely used tools and comparable to the strongest
of them once it is tuned with access to ground-truth labels that SESAA
never sees. In a pilot on real-world Python projects, queries induced
from code available before a vulnerability was introduced detect 10 of
19 subsequent CVEs, including 9 detected by rules written for the same
repository.

The resulting detector is a set of executable, human-readable queries
that engineers can inspect, modify, and run independently. These results
suggest that LLM agents can turn static-analysis rule maintenance from a
manually authored process into an iterative process of automated
discovery and repair.

¹¹footnotetext: Equal second authorship.

Figure 1: Why detectors must evolve. Two near-identical OWASP cases
differ only in how user input reaches the database: (a) concatenates it
into the SQL string (vulnerable), while (b) binds it as a parameter
(safe). A detector that flags any execute() call with nearby tainted
input fires on both — a false positive on (b). Telling them apart
requires understanding the mechanism behind SQL injection and taint
analysis. The user data must reach the _query-string_ argument (argument
1), as sketched in (c). Production-ready queries have to provide this
distinction. However, keeping such rules correct as frameworks, APIs,
and idioms change is a maintenance burden.

Static-analysis tools \[[56](#bib.bib1), [46](#bib.bib11),
[44](#bib.bib12), [24](#bib.bib13)\] are widely used in software
pipelines allowing for scanning source code for security bugs. Security
experts write these tools’ queries by hand and must revise them as
frameworks and codebases change. Each revision requires the expert to
spot a missed vulnerability or a FP (FP). It needs to diagnose why the
rule failed, and rewrite it without breaking what already works (Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
shows one such repair). This process is rather slow and depends heavily
on the expert. A narrow rule misses new patterns, and a broad one
produces the FP that have long held back adoption \[[31](#bib.bib17),
[11](#bib.bib18), [5](#bib.bib19), [45](#bib.bib20)\].

Recent work has started to hand this labour to LLM, asking a model to
read the code and report bugs directly \[[50](#bib.bib5),
[36](#bib.bib58)\] or to write rules from external inputs such as
published CVE reports or fixing patches \[[52](#bib.bib60),
[28](#bib.bib61), [37](#bib.bib62)\]. The first kind leaves little that
can be reused in later scans, while the second ties its findings to
previously documented vulnerabilities. We ask whether an LLM agent can,
instead, maintain its own rules by observing where a rule fails,
diagnosing why, and rewriting it, as a security engineer would.

We present SESAA, an LLM agent that starts with no rules and builds a
set of queries for the open-source analyzer Joern, which represents code
as a searchable graph (Figure
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
The agent operates in rounds, editing its queries and running them over
a body of code that no one has marked as vulnerable or safe.

A second LLM, the critic, reviews what the queries flagged, judges each
finding as a likely bug or a false alarm, and points out places where it
suspects a bug was missed. We call these judgments pseudo-labels,
because they stand in for labels that no one supplies. The run keeps the
set of queries that scores best on them, and no finding is ever checked
against ground-truth labels. The result is an ordinary set of queries
that an engineer can read, edit, and run without the agent
(§[2](#S2 "2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).

#### Contributions.

Our contributions are as follows. (1) SESAA, a framework where an agent
develops and maintains detection queries by evolving them from a
critic’s pseudo-labels, without ground-truth labels. (2) Evolved
detectors that reach a mean $`F_{1}`$ of $`0.742{}`$ over $`8{}`$
independent runs on the OWASP Benchmark for Python \[[41](#bib.bib16)\],
well above the default configurations of five widely used tools and
comparable to CodeQL tuned with access to the labels. (3) A pilot study
on real-world Python projects, in which queries written from code taken
before a vulnerability was introduced flagged 10 of 19 later CVEs.

The remainder of the paper describes the system and its evolutionary
loop
(§[2](#S2 "2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
details the evaluation setup
(§[4](#S4 "4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
reports results
(§[5](#S5 "5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
reviews related work
(§[6](#S6 "6 Related Work ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
discusses the mechanism and threats to validity

§[8](#S8 "8 Threats to Validity ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
and concludes
(§[9](#S9 "9 Conclusion ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).

## 2 System Architecture

Self-Evolving Static Analysis Agent (SESAA), pairs two roles, shown in
Figure
[2](#S2.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling").
The agent writes and repairs detection queries, and the critic, a second
LLM \[[63](#bib.bib9)\], reviews what those queries report. Because no
labels exist to say whether they are right, the critic judges each
finding as a likely true or false positive and turns its doubts into
_tickets_, concrete items for the agent to resolve, either a false alarm
to remove or a suspected miss to close. Starting from an empty set of
queries, the agent repeatedly commits a batch of edits, which we call a
_mutation_, and one committed mutation together with the re-run that
scores it makes up a _generation_. After a fixed budget of generations,
the run returns the best-scoring suite (Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
A security team can read, review, and run the suite independently of the
agent, since it consists of ordinary code and has no dependency on an
LLM.

![Refer to caption](2610.30184v1/figures/andre_sesaa.png)

Figure 2: Overview of SESAA. The ReAct agent repeatedly mutates the
Joern queries and re-runs them over the corpus. A critic pseudo-labels
the reports, estimating precision from every report and rewarding
coverage across vulnerability classes. Ground-truth labels are never
accessible. Over time, queries that receive stronger assessments from
the critic are preferentially retained and propagated.

Code Property Graph and Engine. We build on Joern \[[56](#bib.bib1)\].
Its CPG (CPG) merges syntax ( AST (AST)), execution paths ( CFG (CFG)),
and data and control dependencies ( PDG (PDG)) in one graph, so a single
query can express the taint flows that injection vulnerabilities need.
Every query is ordinary Scala, a general-purpose language the agent can
edit directly. Additionally, it is open source with Python frontend, so
the loop can run it repeatedly over the corpus.

Evolutionary Algorithm. The agent is a ReAct agent \[[59](#bib.bib6)\],
an LLM that alternates between reasoning and calling tools, and in each
generation it acts on the critic’s diagnosis of where the current
queries fail, which lists its tickets and coverage gaps
(§[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Pseudo-Labeled Fitness ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
The difficulty is that every repair risks damage elsewhere, the
stability–plasticity dilemma \[[40](#bib.bib52)\], since a query
tightened to remove one false alarm may stop catching a real bug. Two
things limit that risk. The run keeps the highest-fitness suite seen so
far, so a bad mutation costs one generation and not the run, and the
fitness in
§[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Pseudo-Labeled Fitness ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
penalizes losing either precision or coverage. The repairs that hold up
tend to capture _why_ a flagged case is safe (i.e., it uses escaped
input or a parameterized binding) rather than just narrowing which cases
match, and the agent often records that rationale inline as a comment.
Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
gives the procedure.

The agent has seven tools, which fall into three groups. To act, it has
a shell for running commands, a planning tool for deliberating between
actions, and a query-deletion tool, and it ends each generation with a
commit tool. To check its work, it has a corpus-evaluation tool that
runs the current suite and returns the critic’s scored diagnosis, and a
ticket tool for listing, reviewing, or dismissing false-positive and
false-negative tickets. To consult its own history, it has an
archive-inspection tool that reads prior generations’ suites.

1: Corpus $`C`$; baseline detectors $`D_{0}`$ (all patterns stripped);
message budget $`B`$

2: Agent $`\mathcal{M}_{\pi}`$: a ReAct agent under model $`\pi`$ that
reads the critic’s diagnosis and applies one _mutation_ to the detector

3: Critic
$`\mathcal{K}\!:(D(C),\,C,\,\mathcal{V})\mapsto(\hat{p},\,\hat{c},\,\phi,\,\mathcal{V}^{\prime})`$,
scoring reports without labels and emitting a diagnosis $`\phi`$ (FP

4: Verdict store $`\mathcal{V}`$: persistent per-report verdicts and
tickets (initially $`\varnothing`$)

5: Best detector suite $`D^{\star}`$

6:
$`D\leftarrow D_{0}`$; $`\mathcal{V}\leftarrow\varnothing`$; $`\phi\leftarrow\varnothing`$; $`F^{\star}\leftarrow-\infty`$

so $`B`$ sets how many mutate–evaluate cycles (generations) the run can
perform.

9:   Mutate: the agent applies one mutation, guided by the diagnosis

10:
  $`D\leftarrow\mathcal{M}_{\pi}\big(D,\,C,\,\phi,\,\mathcal{V}\big)`$

### 2.1 Pseudo-Labeled Fitness

The fitness must reward both precision and coverage without ground-truth
labels. We call it _pseudo-labeled_: the critic judges each finding as a
likely TP (TP) or FP from the surrounding code and context, and the
suite’s fitness is aggregated from those judgments. The judgments are
imperfect, since LLM remain unreliable at vulnerability reasoning
\[[15](#bib.bib4)\], so we measure the critic’s accuracy against the
withheld labels
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 RQ2: Does the ticket mechanism behave as designed? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
The signal is therefore weak supervision from a pretrained model, not
supervision-free.

We use these judgments to capture two complementary properties of a
query suite: precision, through the critic’s assessment of individual
findings, and coverage, through the vulnerability classes represented
among those findings.

We formalize this process as follows. Let $`C`$ be the corpus of
applications and $`Q=\{q_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n}`$ a suite of queries. Each
query maps the corpus to a set of _reports_, where a report is one
alert: a code location the query flags as a candidate vulnerability of a
given type. Write $`Q(C)`$ for the pooled reports of the suite. The
fitness $`F(Q)`$ is computed from $`Q(C)`$ and the critic’s verdicts and
tickets on it, never from ground-truth labels.

Estimated precision. The critic assigns every report in $`Q(C)`$ a
verdict, TP or FP, stored in a persistent knowledge base keyed by the
report’s identity and reused in later generations, so findings that
survive a mutation are never re-evaluated. To prevent high-volume
queries from dominating the score, findings are grouped by query and
vulnerability type. For each group ($`g`$), estimated precision is the
fraction of findings judged as TP,
$`\hat{p}_{g}:=\frac{\left|\{r\in g:v(r)=\textsf{TP}\}\right|}{|g|}`$,
where $`v(r)`$ is the stored verdict for report $`r`$. The suite-level
estimated precision is the unweighted mean across groups,
$`\hat{p}:=\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}\hat{p}_{g}.`$

False-positive tickets. Reports the critic marks as FP are surfaced to
the agent as _tickets_: a persistent, per-report list carried across
generations. The agent clears a ticket by tightening the query so the
report is no longer emitted, or by _contesting_ the verdict with an
argument that the report is a TP; a contest re-invokes the critic on
that single report, and the verdict flips only if the critic is
persuaded.

Type coverage. Recall is unobservable without labels, so the fitness
needs a proxy for it. We measure how many distinct vulnerability
_classes_ (SQL injection, path traversal, and so on) the suite
exercises:
$`\hat{c}_{\text{type}}=\frac{\lvert\{\,t\in T:\exists\,r\in Q(C),\;\tau(r)=t\,\}\rvert}{\lvert T\rvert}`$,
where $`T`$ is the target taxonomy and $`\tau(r)`$ a report’s type. This
rewards a suite for covering the classes it targets, not for flagging as
many files as possible, and is indifferent to how vulnerable the corpus
happens to be. For the OWASP evaluation, $`T`$ comprises the benchmark’s
own 14 CWE categories. The agent is never told which files are
vulnerable, but it is told which classes count toward coverage. Its
queries may use a broader 24-type vocabulary recognized by the harness,
including types outside the OWASP taxonomy (e.g., SSRF and IDOR);
unrecognized labels score as unknown with precision $`0`$. Type coverage
measures breadth rather than depth. A class is covered after a single
report, so $`\hat{c}_{\text{type}}`$ saturates once all target classes
are touched, regardless of remaining false negatives. It therefore
provides a useful cold-start signal but no gradient for missed
instances; the FN tickets below provide that signal.

False-negative tickets. FP tickets let the critic audit reported
findings; FN (FN) tickets audit suspected misses, necessarily suspected
since the critic never sees withheld labels
(§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Analyzing the Ticket Mechanism ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
reports how often these suspicions are confirmed). In each generation,
the critic reviews a limited corpus subset, one vulnerability class at a
time, and opens an FN ticket for each vulnerable-looking operation
lacking a report. The agent resolves it by broadening or adding a query,
or by contesting its vulnerability; the critic dismisses the ticket only
if persuaded.

Let $`\mathcal{R}`$ be the FN tickets opened over the reviewed portion
so far, partitioned into resolved and open. Coverage is
$`\hat{c}=\frac{\lvert\mathcal{R}_{\text{resolved}}\rvert}{\lvert\mathcal{R}_{\text{resolved}}\rvert+\lvert\mathcal{R}_{\text{open}}\rvert}`$,
the fraction of critic-identified misses closed so far — a bounded
$`[0,1]`$ recall proxy that rewards each additional recovered instance.
This stays free of ground-truth labels because the denominator ranges
only over what the critic has actually reviewed, and the critic, not the
agent, controls which portions are reviewed, so coverage can only rise
by closing tickets, i.e. by recovering missed vulnerabilities.

Fitness Proxy. Fitness is the geometric mean of the two proxies,
corrected by a single bounded activity term and clamped to $`[0,1]`$:
$`F(Q)\;=\;\min\!\Big(1,\ \sqrt{\hat{p}\cdot\hat{c}}\,\bigl(1+a\bigr)\Big)`$,
where
$`a\;=\;a_{\max}\cdot\min\!\Big(1,\ \frac{|Q(C)|}{n^{\ast}}\Big)`$, with
ceiling $`a_{\max}=0.05`$ and saturation count $`n^{\ast}=10`$ reports.
We use the geometric mean, a standard balanced score under class
imbalance \[[33](#bib.bib27)\]. $`a`$ ramps from $`0`$ to its $`5\%`$
ceiling over a rule’s first ten reports and stays there, a tie-breaker
rewarding output without letting an active-but-worse suite outrank a
better one. Both constants are chosen conservatively, not tuned.

## 3 Illustrative Example

This example follows one early repair through the loop of
§[2](#S2 "2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling").
Like the SQL case in Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling"),
the XPath-injection query relied on a coarse taint rule that could not
tell why a construct was safe, so it raised FP on benign code.

The critic doubts a finding. After a generation, the critic reviews what
the XPath query flagged. It never sees a label, so it judges each
finding from the surrounding code and opens a FP ticket for the findings
that look benign, here calls that pass their values as bound parameters
or escape them first.

The agent repairs the query. The agent reads the ticketed cases and the
code around them, identifies two safe idioms, and adds an exclusion for
each to the query (Figure
[3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3 Illustrative Example ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
The query now ignores calls whose query literal contains an escape
entity and calls that use a name= binding. The edit captures _why_ these
cases are safe, and the agent records that rationale in an inline
comment.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

cpg.call.name("xpath\|select")

- // exclude XML-escaped queries (value neutralised)

- .filterNot(c =\> c.method.ast.isLiteral

- .code(".\*&apos;.\*\|.\*&quot;.\*").nonEmpty)

- // exclude parameterized binding: xpath(q, name=...)

- .filterNot(c =\> c.code.matches(".\*\\bname\\s\*=.\*"))

.filter(c =\> c.argument

.reachableByFlows(SOURCES).nonEmpty)

Figure 3: Semantic repair to the XPath-injection query. The agent’s edit
(green) adds two exclusions to the original rule (black): XML-escaped
arguments and calls that pass values via a named parameter (name=...)
rather than concatenation.

The suite is scored again. The agent commits the mutation, and the
corpus-evaluation tool re-runs every query over the code property graph
and rescores the findings (Algorithm
[1](#alg1 "Algorithm 1 ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
With the escaped and parameterized cases excluded, the XPath group’s
estimated precision rises, the fitness improves over the best suite so
far, and the run keeps the new suite
(§[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Pseudo-Labeled Fitness ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).

What the example shows. The repair is small, and it is the kind an
engineer would make. It separates safe constructs from unsafe ones and
does not suppress the query, and the rationale comments make the change
reviewable without the agent. The exchange can also run the other way,
as in the ticket of
§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 RQ2: Does the ticket mechanism behave as designed? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
where the agent contests the critic’s verdict and the critic reverses
it, so the signal that drives the repair is checked from both sides.

## 4 Methodology

This section describes our experimental setup: the evaluation corpus
(§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Evaluation Corpus ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
the baseline and agent configuration
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Evolution Configuration ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
the models we use
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Models ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
the experimental settings
(§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Experimental Settings ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
the metrics we use to evaluate the evolved detectors
(§[4.5](#S4.SS5 "4.5 Evaluation Metrics ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
the protocol for analyzing the ticket mechanism
(§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Analyzing the Ticket Mechanism ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
the statistical tests
(§[4.7](#S4.SS7 "4.7 Statistical Tests ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
and the introduction-time detection dataset
(§[4.8](#S4.SS8 "4.8 Introduction-Time Detection Dataset ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).

### 4.1 Evaluation Corpus

We evaluate SESAA on the OWASP Benchmark for Python
\[[41](#bib.bib16)\], a synthetic suite where each file contains exactly
one test case labeled vulnerable or safe. It spans 14 vulnerability
categories and 1,230 test cases in total, 452 vulnerable and 778 safe.
We evaluate one language, Python, with 8 S1 seeds and three ablations.

We extend the evaluation to a small corpus of real-world Python
projects, each containing at least one known vulnerability. Each
repository appears in two states: a pre-vulnerability snapshot, against
which the agent writes its own queries, and a post-vulnerability
snapshot, against which we check whether those queries flag the
introduced vulnerability.

### 4.2 Evolution Configuration

We report a single configuration of SESAA’s loop. We choose a Claude
Sonnet 5 \[[3](#bib.bib28)\] agent paired with an Claude Opus 4.8
\[[2](#bib.bib29)\] critic
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Models ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
evolving detectors on the OWASP Benchmark for Python, orchestrated with
the Inspect AI framework \[[51](#bib.bib26)\]. The loop starts from a
workspace with all detection patterns stripped, forcing the agent to
discover detectors from scratch rather than tuning an existing suite.

Generations and mutations. A _mutation_ is the change the agent commits
to the detector suite by writing, editing, or deleting Joern queries. A
_generation_ is one committed mutation, after which the suite is re-run
and scored. Before committing, the agent may edit, measure the result,
and read the critic’s feedback as many times as it likes.

Budget and determinism. Each generation’s react loop is bounded by a
budget of 2000 messages, stated verbatim in the system prompt, after
which the workspace is auto-committed even if the agent never explicitly
commits. Ground-truth labels are never placed in the agent’s context or
tool results. We compute the true $`F_{1}`$ separately, purely for the
evaluation of
§[5](#S5 "5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling").
We write the critic’s per-finding verdicts once into a persistent store
and reuse them whenever a finding survives a mutation unchanged, so
re-evaluating an untouched detector does not re-invoke the judge.

Baselines. We run a panel of widely used static and dynamic-analysis
tools, CodeQL \[[24](#bib.bib13)\], Semgrep \[[46](#bib.bib11)\], Bandit
\[[44](#bib.bib12)\], Bearer \[[4](#bib.bib14)\], and OWASP ZAP
\[[42](#bib.bib15)\], each in two configurations, scored with the
official OWASP scorecard. The out-of-the-box configuration runs the
community queries. CodeQL uses the _python-security-extended_ suite with
the GitHub Security Lab pack, and Semgrep uses the community packs
_p/python_, _p/flask_, _p/secrets_, _p/security-audit_, and
_p/owasp-top-ten_. The tuned configuration upgrades those community
queries by having an LLM agent evolve them against the withheld labels.
We run this tuning with three backbones (Claude Sonnet 5, Kimi-K2.5,
GLM-5) at three window sizes (30, 60, 100 retained messages), for 9
tuning runs per tool. We report the best-performing queries from each
tool’s 9-run panel, scored against the withheld OWASP labels after
tuning. Unlike SESAA, which never observes the withheld labels at any
point, the best-of-9 selection for every baseline tool is made _with_
access to them. SESAA matching or exceeding a baseline tuned this way is
therefore evidence under a harder information constraint, not a
like-for-like accuracy race
(§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 RQ3: Do static-analysis queries evolved without ground-truth labels reach the quality of mature, hand-maintained SAST tools? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).

We run the same 3-backbone $`\times`$ 3-window panel with Joern itself
as a sixth baseline. A single agent turn writes queries directly against
the withheld labels, with no critic, tickets, or further generations,
and we report the best of the 9 configurations. Joern ships no built-in
ruleset, so an empty out-of-the-box query set would trivially score zero
rather than a weaker-but-nonzero point.

### 4.3 Models

The task demands a backbone fluent in both Python and Scala. We use
Claude Sonnet 5 \[[3](#bib.bib28)\] as the agent, chosen for its strong
code-generation and agentic performance \[[60](#bib.bib31),
[8](#bib.bib30), [30](#bib.bib32)\], and the more capable Claude Opus
4.8 \[[2](#bib.bib29)\] as the critic, mirroring a realistic deployment
where a cheaper model handles high-volume exploration while a more
capable model adjudicates the smaller set of findings it surfaces.

### 4.4 Experimental Settings

We organize the evaluation into five settings, identified throughout as
S1–S5 and summarized visually in Figure
[4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ S4: removing FN tickets leaves the mean unchanged but widens the spread. ‣ 5.1 RQ1: Can static-analysis queries evolve without ground-truth labels, from scratch? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling").
S1 is the configuration of
§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Evolution Configuration ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling"),
repeated across 8 independent runs to quantify the variance of a
stochastic loop
(§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 RQ1: Can static-analysis queries evolve without ground-truth labels, from scratch? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
S2 to S4 are ablations, each run with five independent seeds, that
remove one component at a time while holding the corpus, message budget,
tooling, and model pair fixed, so the difference in ground-truth quality
measures the contribution of the removed component. S5 moves the loop to
a corpus of real-world Python projects.

In S2, the agent keeps its budget, tools, and corpus and still sees the
raw findings of its queries, but receives no critic verdicts, tickets,
or fitness. The returned suite is chosen exactly as in S1, so S2
measures what an agent achieves by writing and running detectors alone.
S3 keeps the critic’s precision estimate but removes the itemized FP
tickets and contest step of
§[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Pseudo-Labeled Fitness ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling"),
isolating the ticket surface’s contribution from that of the score it
feeds. S4 removes the FN tickets, so coverage reverts to the
presence-based $`\hat{c}_{\text{type}}`$, which changes both the ticket
surface and the recall term of the fitness.

S5 keeps the critic and the tickets and changes the corpus and the
fitness proxy. Pre-introduction snapshots contain no vulnerabilities, so
precision and recall against labeled findings are undefined and the
proactive fitness of
§[4.8](#S4.SS8 "4.8 Introduction-Time Detection Dataset ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
replaces them. S5 therefore tests whether an agent that reasons over
clean code writes queries that catch vulnerabilities introduced later,
not whether the fitness design of
§[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Pseudo-Labeled Fitness ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
holds on real code.

### 4.5 Evaluation Metrics

We report precision, recall, $`F_{1}`$, and Youden’s J computed per
finding against the withheld labels. These labels are assigned a priori
and are never visible to the agent. Precision is the share of a suite’s
alerts that point at a real vulnerability, so a precision of 0.8 means
four of every five alerts are real. Recall is the share of the
benchmark’s vulnerable test cases that the suite flags. The $`F_{1}`$ is
their harmonic mean and is high only when both are high. Youden’s $`J`$
is the true-positive rate minus the false-positive rate, so a suite that
flags every file scores zero. The benchmark has 452 vulnerable and 778
safe test cases, so a suite that flags nothing has zero recall and one
that flags everything has a false-positive rate of one. For the
introduction-time benchmark
(§[4.8](#S4.SS8 "4.8 Introduction-Time Detection Dataset ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
we report whether the suite detects the vulnerability at the commit that
introduces it, and whether the ticket mechanism then corrects any
resulting FP.

### 4.6 Analyzing the Ticket Mechanism

One of SESAA’s central components is the ticket mechanism, which lets
the critic flag a finding and the agent repair or contest it. We fix the
protocol for one of two separate questions: whether the mechanism
_behaves as designed_, meaning the critic’s judgment tracks ground truth
and the agent acts on it. The other question, whether _having_ the
mechanism _improves the detector_, is answered separately by the S3
ablation (defined in
§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Experimental Settings ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling");
results in
§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 RQ1: Can static-analysis queries evolve without ground-truth labels, from scratch? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
and by the S4 ablation for FN tickets, which compare outcomes with the
ticket surface on versus off across independent seeds.

#### Labeling tickets against ground truth.

Checking whether a ticket is accurate requires knowing whether the
finding behind it is a genuine FP, so we check every opened ticket and
every repair made against the withheld labels. The critic opens a ticket
for each finding it judges a FP. The agent may then repair the query or
contest the ticket, and the critic accepts or rejects the contest. We
label each ticketed finding as a genuine FP or a real vulnerability,
judging both whether the critic’s ticket (and contest verdict) is
correct, and whether the agent’s repair removed a genuine FP or
destroyed a real detection.

### 4.7 Statistical Tests

The ticket mechanism setup raises three questions. First, whether a FP
ticket actually points at a genuine FP. Second, whether repairs
concentrate on the tickets the critic flagged rather than falling just
as likely on anything else. Third, whether the critic’s precision
estimate is systematically biased relative to the withheld ground truth.
For each, we compute the null distribution by exact enumeration rather
than a normal approximation. We compute Fisher’s exact test
\[[18](#bib.bib33)\] for the first question (whether FP tickets are
independent of ground-truth FP status), a one-sided hypergeometric test
for the second (random draw versus selective response), and an exact
Wilcoxon signed-rank test \[[54](#bib.bib34), [23](#bib.bib35)\] for the
third.

We perform two additional checks of the mechanism’s overall behavior.
First, we test whether the critic’s fitness score tracks the withheld
ground truth over the full run, using Pearson correlation with a
$`t`$-test on the coefficient \[[49](#bib.bib36)\] and Spearman
correlation to assess rank agreement. Second, we test whether the
critic’s judgment extends to the recall side by comparing the fraction
of FN tickets that correspond to real vulnerabilities against the
per-class base rate of a random file, using a one-sided Fisher exact
test \[[18](#bib.bib33)\].

For ablation comparisons
(§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Experimental Settings ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
Welch’s $`t`$-test compares each ablation’s mean F1 against S1, the
reported configuration repeated across seeds
(§[4.4](#S4.SS4 "4.4 Experimental Settings ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
For the ticket mechanism, we compute each test above per-seed, then
combine across seeds via Fisher’s method (a $`\chi^{2}`$-test on pooled
$`p`$-values). Fisher’s method still assumes the 8 per-seed $`p`$-values
are independent, which holds because each seed is an independently
seeded run, though not _within_ a seed’s tickets.

Bayesian supplement for the ablations. Each independent evolution run
costs on the order of hundreds of dollars in API spend, so each ablation
arm has only $`n{=}5`$ seeds, small enough that a $`p`$-value above 0.05
is easy to misread as “no effect” when it may just mean the test is
underpowered
(§[8](#S8 "8 Threats to Validity ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
As a supplement, we instead report a Bayesian estimate of each
ablation’s standardized effect size, Cohen’s $`d`$ for ablation vs. S1.
We use a weakly informative prior, $`\mathcal{N}(0,1)`$, centered on _no
effect_, updated against the observed $`d`$ and its standard error
\[[27](#bib.bib59)\] via the standard Normal-Normal conjugate rule. This
provides a posterior over the true effect size and, from it, the
posterior probability that the true effect runs in the predicted,
harmful, direction. The prior pulls each posterior back toward zero
relative to the raw observed effect.

### 4.8 Introduction-Time Detection Dataset

The S5 corpus enables us to evaluate whether queries developed on clean
code catch a vulnerability at the moment it is introduced. We resolve
this for CVEs in our real-world corpus via SZZ-style blame attribution
\[[48](#bib.bib53)\]: for each fix commit we trace its changed lines
backward through git blame to their introducing commit, with automatic
escalation from shallow to full history when a boundary is hit.

We resolve 36 files covering 19 CVEs across 12 Python projects. Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.8 Introduction-Time Detection Dataset ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
gives the per-repository breakdown. By vulnerability type across all 12
projects, we cover path traversal, XSS, code injection, SQL injection,
and command injection.

For each resolved case, we export the codebase immediately before and
after the introducing commit, and record which file, function, and line
ranges that commit added, matching at function granularity for 109 of
133 introduced ranges and falling back to line-level for the rest. Since
multiple CVEs may be introduced at different points in a repository’s
history, we create one snapshot per unique introducing commit. The full
per-CVE listing (repository, CWE type, commit, date, used-for-training
flag) is in the released benchmark artifact.

| Repo                | Type               | CVEs | Caught |
| ------------------- | ------------------ | ---- | ------ |
| mistune (2 runs)    | XSS/Path Trav      | 4    | 4      |
| prompty             | Path Trav          | 1    | 1      |
| Pillow              | Cmd Inj            | 1    | 1      |
| langroid            | Path+SQL           | 1    | 1      |
| litellm (untrained) | Code Inj/Path Trav | 2    | 0      |
| picklescan          | Code Inj           | 1    | 1      |
| keras               | Path Trav          | 2    | 0      |
| open-webui          | Path Trav          | 1    | 1      |
| MobSF               | XSS                | 2    | 0      |
| llama_index         | SQL Inj            | 1    | 0      |
| pyload              | Code Inj           | 1    | 1^(†)  |
| changedetection.io  | XSS                | 2    | 0      |

Table 1: Per-repository breakdown of the full 12-project S5 corpus.
^(†)pyload’s own detector missed its CVE; it was caught only via
cross-repository transfer from the open-webui and changedetection.io
detectors
(§[5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 RQ4 (pilot study): Can agents write proactive security rules on clean code that catch vulnerabilities at introduction time? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
Totals: 19 CVEs, 10 caught (53%).

#### S5 experimental protocol.

For each S5 run, we evolve detectors on one pre-introduction tree, a
repository snapshot captured immediately before a
vulnerability-introducing commit was applied, testing whether agents can
write proactive security queries on clean code that catch
vulnerabilities once later introduced, without having seen any
vulnerable examples. Pre-introduction trees contain no instance of the
CVE they are tested on, providing no traditional training signal. Agents
must instead identify security-sensitive code patterns, such as file
I/O, SQL query construction, shell command execution, path manipulation,
and HTML rendering, and write queries that flag potential violations
based on best practices rather than concrete examples. The fitness
function for pre-introduction evolution is
$`F_{\text{proactive}}=\hat{c}_{\text{pattern}}\times(1-\hat{r}_{\text{fp}}),`$
where $`\hat{c}_{\text{pattern}}`$ is the fraction of detected
security-sensitive patterns covered by evolved queries, and
$`\hat{r}_{\text{fp}}`$ the critic-judged false-positive rate of the
queries’ findings on the clean training corpus.

We evolve detectors on each pre-introduction snapshot, then test the
resulting suite against introduction cases, mimicking a project-specific
SAST tool evolving continuously and flagging newly introduced code. A
detection counts as a hit if the evolved suite fires on a finding
matching the reported CVE. The resulting benchmark, 36 test cases
spanning 19 CVEs across 12 projects, is released for evaluating any SAST
tool on introduction-time recall.

## 5 Results

We ask four questions of the evolved detectors. The first is whether
detection queries can evolve from an empty start without ground-truth
labels, and they can
(§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 RQ1: Can static-analysis queries evolve without ground-truth labels, from scratch? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
The second is whether the critic and its tickets behave as designed. The
critic’s flags are enriched for real FP and the agent’s repairs follow
them above chance
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 RQ2: Does the ticket mechanism behave as designed? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
The third is how the queries compare with mature tools
(§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 RQ3: Do static-analysis queries evolved without ground-truth labels reach the quality of mature, hand-maintained SAST tools? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
The fourth, a pilot, is whether queries written on clean code catch
vulnerabilities introduced later
(§[5.5](#S5.SS5 "5.5 RQ4 (pilot study): Can agents write proactive security rules on clean code that catch vulnerabilities at introduction time? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).

### 5.1 RQ1: Can static-analysis queries evolve without ground-truth labels, from scratch?

We run 8 independent evolution sessions from an empty starting point,
varying only the random seed, and score each returned suite against the
withheld labels. Precision is the share of a suite’s alerts that are
real, and recall is the share of the benchmark’s vulnerabilities it
finds. The mean $`F_{1}`$, which balances the two, is $`0.742{}`$, from
a mean precision of $`0.780{}`$ and a mean recall of $`0.734{}`$. The
runs differ because the loop is stochastic and we do not control
decoding settings, with a standard deviation of $`0.084{}`$ and a 95%
confidence interval of $`[0.671{},0.812{}]`$. Against the strongest
baseline, 6 of 8 seeds exceed CodeQL’s $`F_{1}`$ of 0.70 (Figure
[4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ S4: removing FN tickets leaves the mean unchanged but widens the spread. ‣ 5.1 RQ1: Can static-analysis queries evolve without ground-truth labels, from scratch? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
and the other two fall below it, so the mean sits only modestly above
the baseline and its interval overlaps CodeQL’s score.

Figure
[4](#S5.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ S4: removing FN tickets leaves the mean unchanged but widens the spread. ‣ 5.1 RQ1: Can static-analysis queries evolve without ground-truth labels, from scratch? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
shows the three ablations against S1.

#### S2: removing the critic raises the false-positive rate, without moving $`F_{1}`$ significantly.

With no critic output, precision falls from $`0.780{}`$ to $`0.642{}`$
($`p=0.075{}`$) as the agent writes looser detectors with nothing to
prune FP, while recall rises from $`0.734{}`$ to $`0.825{}`$
($`p=0.127{}`$). The $`F_{1}`$ drop does not reach significance
($`p=0.478{}`$) at this sample size because the precision loss and
recall gain partly cancel in the harmonic mean.

#### S3: removing FP tickets trends worse on every metric.

S3 is the closest of the three ablations to significance on $`F_{1}`$
($`p=0.091{}`$). Youden’s $`J`$ ($`p=0.155{}`$), precision
($`p=0.274{}`$), and recall ($`p=0.244{}`$) all trend the same
direction, consistent with the FP-ticket mechanism costing detector
quality broadly rather than trading one axis for another.

#### S4: removing FN tickets leaves the mean unchanged but widens the spread.

Only the pointer to likely-missed vulnerabilities is removed; the
critic’s precision estimate, FP tickets, and fitness score are
unchanged. Precision and recall drift the same way as in S2 but more
weakly (recall $`p=0.304{}`$, precision $`p=0.245{}`$), and the
$`F_{1}`$ difference is not significant ($`p=0.468{}`$).

None of the three individually establishes that the mechanism drives
$`F_{1}`$, so we treat them as directionally consistent, not as proof.
Pooling all three via Fisher’s combined probability test
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 RQ2: Does the ticket mechanism behave as designed? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")’s
pooling method) leaves that conclusion unchanged on $`F_{1}`$
($`\chi^{2}=7.79{}`$, $`\mathit{df}=6`$, $`p=0.254{}`$) but moves closer
to significance on precision ($`\chi^{2}=10.58{}`$, $`p=0.102{}`$), a
real but modest effect that three $`n{=}5`$ ablations remain
underpowered to establish alone.

As
§[4.7](#S4.SS7 "4.7 Statistical Tests ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
describes, we supplement the frequentist tests with a Bayesian
effect-size estimate under a skeptical prior. S3 keeps most of its
signal: from $`d=-1.05{}`$ to $`d=-0.77{}\pm 0.52{}`$, with 93%
posterior probability the effect is real and harmful. S2 and S4 shrink
further, landing at more modest posterior effects
($`-0.31{}\pm 0.50{}`$, 73%; $`-0.34{}\pm 0.50{}`$, 75%). The controlled
evidence that the critic/ticket mechanism does what it is designed to do
comes from directly testing its behavior, not from these outcome
ablations.
§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 RQ2: Does the ticket mechanism behave as designed? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
does that next.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Ground-truth performance by setting. S1 matches the best
baseline tool, and removing any one mechanism lowers the mean on both
metrics, though not significantly at this sample size
(§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 RQ1: Can static-analysis queries evolve without ground-truth labels, from scratch? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
Ground-truth $`F_{1}`$ and Youden’s $`J`$ by setting, against the best
baseline tool, mean $`\pm`$ 95% CI over independent seeds. Youden’s
$`J=`$ sensitivity $`+`$ specificity $`-1`$; for the evolved detector,
TN are approximated as corpus-safe files minus FP (an upper bound on
$`J`$), whereas the baseline tool’s $`J`$ is computed from exact TN, so
the two are not on strictly equal footing.

### 5.2 RQ2: Does the ticket mechanism behave as designed?

The critic opens a ticket for each finding it doubts, and the agent
either repairs the query so the finding disappears or contests the
ticket
(§[2](#S2 "2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
We check this mechanism against the withheld ground truth across all 8
S1 seeds. We ask whether the critic flags findings that really are false
alarms, whether the agent repairs those more often than chance would
predict, and whether the critic’s estimate of its own precision is fair.
Exact tests answer each in turn
(§[4.6](#S4.SS6 "4.6 Analyzing the Ticket Mechanism ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling"),
§[4.7](#S4.SS7 "4.7 Statistical Tests ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).

The critic’s tickets are enriched for real FP, and the agent acts on
that signal. Removing a ticketed finding that is a FP raises $`F_{1}`$,
but removing one that is a real vulnerability lowers it, so we focus
here on whether the critic identifies genuine FP, and whether the agent
repairs those more than it would by chance.

#### A concrete example.

The critic opened a ticket for random.randbytes(32) generating a
rememberMe session cookie, judging 256 bits of PRNG output sufficient
with no attacker-controlled seed apparent. The agent contested. Absent
an explicit SystemRandom instance, random.randbytes() relies on Python’s
Mersenne Twister, the exact CWE-330 pattern the benchmark’s sibling
weakrand cases target. The critic re-judged, agreed, and reversed the
ticket to confirmed vulnerability (Figure
[5](#S5.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ A concrete example. ‣ 5.2 RQ2: Does the ticket mechanism behave as designed? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
This exchange is taken from one archived run. The same pattern of doubt,
repair or contest, and resolution recurs across the 2158 tickets
summarized below, most resolving with less back-and-forth.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: The exchange behind the ticket in the concrete example above:
the critic’s first read, the agent’s contest, and the critic’s reversal.

Across all 8 S1 seeds, the agent opened 2158 tickets covering 1108
distinct findings and repaired 665 of them, where a ticket counts as
solved once the agent’s repair removes its finding. Of those, 568 were
genuine FP and 97 were real vulnerabilities removed by mistake, a pooled
solve precision of 85%. Seed by seed, the precision is
$`89\%{}\pm 0.11{}`$, with a range of 68%–100%.

Figure 6: Ticket mechanism outcomes, pooled and per-seed across all 8 S1
runs, scored against the withheld labels. Left: outcome for each
ticketed finding by ground-truth label; of 665 findings solved in total,
568 were genuine FP and 97 were real vulnerabilities removed by mistake.
Right: ground-truth $`F_{1}`$ under three repair strategies (ignore
every ticket, the agent’s actual selective repairs, blindly clear every
open ticket), plotted per seed; in every seed, being selective beats
both extremes.

Across all 8 runs, blindly clearing every open ticket (fixing FP and
real vulnerabilities alike, with no selectivity) scores _below_ the
agent’s actual, selective repairs (Figure
[6](#S5.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ A concrete example. ‣ 5.2 RQ2: Does the ticket mechanism behave as designed? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).

Targeting. A ticketed finding is more likely to be a genuine FP. A
per-seed Fisher’s exact test is significant on 7/8 seeds, and combining
all 8 ($`p=1.1\times 10^{-35}{}`$) rejects the null that tickets are
independent of FP status.

Selection. The agent’s repair choice tracks that signal rather than
ignoring it. A per-seed one-sided hypergeometric test is significant on
8/8 seeds, and combined ($`p=5.2\times 10^{-71}{}`$) shows the agent
repairs more genuine FP than chance would predict, listening to the
critic in every run.

Calibration. The critic’s own precision estimate is conservative. Across
all 8 seeds, the direction never flips, underrating its detectors on
average (0.19, SD 0.07, range 0.11–0.26), though only 4/8 of the
per-seed Wilcoxon tests clear conventional significance alone.

Across 8 independent trajectories, the critic’s tickets point
disproportionately at genuine FP, the agent acts on that signal, and
where the critic is wrong about its own accuracy, it errs on the safe
side.

False-negative tickets. The FN tickets do the same job for recall. A
one-sided Fisher’s exact test is significant on 8/8 seeds, pooling to
159 FN tickets, of which a pooled share of 61% point at a genuine miss
(mean 70% $`\pm`$ 17% averaged seed by seed), pointing the agent toward
the higher-risk part of the corpus despite seed-to-seed variance.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5.3 Agent Behaviour

Across the $`711{}`$ tool calls of the committed generation, the agent
edits existing detectors ($`85{}`$ calls) far more often than it writes
new ones from scratch ($`37{}`$), and spends the bulk of its budget
reading and exploring the corpus before touching a query at all. Figure
[7](#S5.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 5.3 Agent Behaviour ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
shows this is not one habit sustained throughout but a rhythm repeated
every generation: explore and read, then a burst of editing, then an
evaluation call that closes the loop and starts the next round.

Compute cost. One S1 run uses around $`254M{}`$ input and $`490K{}`$
output Claude Sonnet 5 tokens for the agent, plus at least $`1.68M{}`$
input and $`213K{}`$ output Claude Opus 4.8 tokens for the critic.

Figure 7: Agent activity composition across the committed generation
(single session; commands classified by shape). Faint vertical ticks
mark each evaluation against the corpus.

### 5.4 RQ3: Do static-analysis queries evolved without ground-truth labels reach the quality of mature, hand-maintained SAST tools?

A detector that only beats an empty baseline is not useful in practice,
so we compare against the tools practitioners already use. The panel is
five widely used tools (CodeQL, Semgrep, Bandit, Bearer, OWASP ZAP),
each tuned with access to the withheld labels that SESAA never sees,
plus a one-shot LLM-written Joern baseline that shows what the evolution
loop adds
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Evolution Configuration ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
Each tool contributes a single best-of-9 score, and its tuning budget is
not matched to SESAA’s.

(a) Performance breakdown, tuned and community configurations.

(b) Recall versus FPR.

Figure 8: Comparison with baseline tools. The evolved detector’s
precision-recall tradeoff sits closest to the upper-left of any tool in
the panel, driven mainly by precision rather than recall
(§[5.4](#S5.SS4 "5.4 RQ3: Do static-analysis queries evolved without ground-truth labels reach the quality of mature, hand-maintained SAST tools? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
(a) Recall, precision, and $`F_{1}`$ for each tool; CodeQL, Semgrep, and
Bandit show both community and tuned configurations (Bearer/ZAP ship one
configuration; Joern has no out-of-the-box ruleset, so only its best
one-shot LLM configuration is shown). (b) Recall versus FPR for each
tool’s strongest (tuned) configuration; the evolved Joern detector is
plotted once per S1 seed (light stars) and once as a
median-FPR/mean-recall summary (dark star); the diamond marker is the
best one-shot LLM-written Joern ruleset. Points closer to the upper-left
are preferable.

The evolved detector reaches the highest mean $`F_{1}`$ of the panel
($`0.742{}\pm 0.084{}`$), ahead of tuned CodeQL ($`0.70{}`$), the
strongest baseline, and of every other tool (Figure
[8](#S5.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 5.4 RQ3: Do static-analysis queries evolved without ground-truth labels reach the quality of mature, hand-maintained SAST tools? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
including the one-shot Joern ruleset ($`0.69{}`$). The margin over
CodeQL is small and the 8-seed 95% confidence interval overlaps CodeQL’s
score, so the fair reading is that the evolved queries match the best
tuned tool without ever seeing a label.

The advantage over CodeQL comes mainly from precision. Mean recall
($`0.734{}`$) is close to CodeQL’s ($`0.74{}`$), while mean precision is
$`0.780{}`$, and the two highest-precision tools, Bearer and ZAP, reach
theirs by giving up most of their coverage. The community,
out-of-the-box configurations of CodeQL, Semgrep, and Bandit score well
below their tuned versions ($`0.30{}`$, $`0.19{}`$, $`0.37{}`$), and the
evolved detector clears them by a wide margin.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### 5.5 RQ4 (pilot study): Can agents write proactive security rules on clean code that catch vulnerabilities at introduction time?

Previous RQs have focused on reactive detection. We now ask whether an
agent in the same setting can write detectors that catch vulnerabilities
proactively, at the moment they are introduced. We ask this as a
question about the agent’s zero-shot reasoning, not about whether
SESAA’s evolutionary fitness mechanism specifically drives it: the two
come apart in this pilot, and we treat that separation as a finding in
its own right.

We evolve detectors on real-world repositories’ pre-introduction
snapshots, using the pattern-coverage fitness of
§[4.8](#S4.SS8 "4.8 Introduction-Time Detection Dataset ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
(no precision/recall signal is available on a corpus with zero
vulnerabilities by construction), then test the resulting suite against
the actual introducing commit.

We report this as a pilot study on a benchmark we release for it.
Zero-shot agentic reasoning caught 10 of the 19 CVEs in this sample.

Each detector is tested only on introduction cases from the repository
whose snapshot it was evolved on, except where noted as cross-repository
transfer.

#### The capability result: detection succeeded more often than not.

Across all 12 runs, evolved detectors caught 10 of 19 CVEs. Table
[1](#S4.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 4.8 Introduction-Time Detection Dataset ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
gives the full per-repository breakdown. 9 of the 10 catches came from a
detector evolved on the same repository, out of 17 CVEs in trained
repositories. litellm, the one repository without a training run, was
missed on both of its CVEs, and keras, MobSF, llama_index, and
changedetection.io caught none of their own CVEs. The remaining catch is
a cross-repository transfer: pyload’s own detector missed its CVE while
the open-webui and changedetection.io detectors both flagged it, direct
evidence that a rule evolved on one codebase can generalize to a
vulnerability pattern in an entirely different one.

The lowest-scoring repositories are also among the largest and most
complex (llama_index has 3,893 files, while keras and MobSF each run in
the hundreds), while picklescan, the smallest at 7 files, was detected
perfectly. We flag this only as an observed correlation across a
12-repository sample, not a tested hypothesis, since we have not
measured what drives it.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## 6 Related Work

SESAA sits between several ways of finding software vulnerabilities, and
inherits from each without fully belonging to any of them. Static
analyzers such as Joern \[[56](#bib.bib1), [55](#bib.bib2)\], CodeQL
\[[24](#bib.bib13)\], Semgrep \[[46](#bib.bib11)\], and Infer
\[[6](#bib.bib37)\] expose programmable queries over syntax, control
flow, and data flow, and stay deterministic and explainable only as long
as those queries keep up with how languages and frameworks actually
change, a maintenance burden that grows with deployment scale
\[[5](#bib.bib19)\]. SESAA keeps that same deterministic query as its
output, but rewrites it continuously, guided by a critic’s pseudo-labels
rather than a human maintainer.

A parallel line of work sidesteps rule maintenance by learning to
classify vulnerable code directly: Devign \[[64](#bib.bib39)\], SySeVR
\[[38](#bib.bib40)\], ReVeal \[[7](#bib.bib41)\], LineVul
\[[19](#bib.bib42)\], and pretrained encoders such as GraphCodeBERT
\[[26](#bib.bib43)\] all reach strong predictive accuracy this way, but
the result is a classifier rather than an analysis, and what these
models learn stays in their weights rather than in a query a security
engineer can read, edit, or run on its own.

LLM agents for software security. LLM agents push further in the same
direction, applying language models directly to vulnerability detection
\[[22](#bib.bib3), [15](#bib.bib4), [50](#bib.bib5), [16](#bib.bib64)\],
code review \[[12](#bib.bib54)\], repair \[[34](#bib.bib55)\], exploit
generation \[[17](#bib.bib56)\], and penetration testing
\[[14](#bib.bib57)\], with agentic tool use adding iterative execution
feedback \[[59](#bib.bib6), [58](#bib.bib21), [62](#bib.bib44)\];
Codebadger, for instance, exposes Joern’s CPG to an agent through
slicing and taint-tracking tools rather than raw queries
\[[36](#bib.bib58)\]. Here the model is doing the analysis itself, on
every repository and every run, so little of what it learns carries over
to the next one, even where a second model checks its work, as in recent
verifier-style vulnerability discovery \[[29](#bib.bib10)\]. SESAA also
uses a second model this way, as an LLM-as-judge \[[63](#bib.bib9)\],
but points the resulting signal at the query rather than the verdict, so
what persists across runs is the analyzer rather than a transcript.

LLM-generated analysis rules. A closer line of work has LLM write the
rules themselves. QLCoder synthesizes CodeQL queries from CVE metadata
and vulnerable and patched code, refining each query with execution
feedback \[[52](#bib.bib60)\]. Irsan et al. generate CodeQL queries from
National Vulnerability Database entries \[[28](#bib.bib61)\], and MoCQ
refines LLM-written vulnerability patterns against symbolic validation
feedback \[[37](#bib.bib62)\]. These systems take their supervision from
outside, as CVE reports, patches, or pattern specifications, whereas
SESAA takes it from a critic’s pseudo-labels over unlabeled code and
keeps evolving the same detector across generations.

Self-improving software engineering agents. Reflexion
\[[47](#bib.bib45)\], Self-Refine \[[39](#bib.bib46)\], TextGrad
\[[61](#bib.bib47)\], OPRO \[[57](#bib.bib48)\], and GEPA
\[[1](#bib.bib49)\] face a related problem from the agent’s side: they
get better at reasoning through refined prompts, strategies, or
policies, but that improvement stays embedded in the model pipeline and
inherits continual learning’s stability-plasticity dilemma
\[[25](#bib.bib38), [40](#bib.bib52)\].

Evolutionary search and neuroevolution. The archive-and-mutation loop
underneath SESAA is closer to genetic programming’s evolution of
executable programs \[[32](#bib.bib22)\] and neuroevolution’s search
beyond fixed parameters \[[20](#bib.bib23), [13](#bib.bib24)\], both of
which justify branching, non-greedy search over an irregular landscape.
Recent surveys extend that idea to LLM-based systems
\[[21](#bib.bib25)\]: Meta-Harness evolves the harness around a fixed
model \[[35](#bib.bib7)\], and HarnessX treats the harness itself,
prompts, tools, memory, control flow, as a composable artefact
\[[9](#bib.bib8)\]. SESAA shares the premise that the machinery around a
model is worth evolving, but points it at the analysis logic itself,
selected by a critic-pseudo-labeled signal that needs no ground truth,
with a feedback step that draws on Reflexion, Self-Refine
\[[47](#bib.bib45), [39](#bib.bib46)\], and GEPA’s critique/generation
split \[[1](#bib.bib49)\].

## 7 Discussion

The critic is the agent’s only source of feedback. The tickets are
enriched for genuine FP, and the agent repairs those more often than
chance would predict. Both effects are significant across seeds. The
outcome ablations point the same way. Removing the critic, the FP
tickets, or the FN tickets each lowers the mean $`F_{1}`$, and the
Bayesian estimate puts 93% posterior probability on the FP-ticket
removal being harmful. These differences are not individually
significant, so we read them as a consistent direction whose size a
larger campaign would pin down. At the same time, the agent writes
strong detectors without the critic. The critic’s contribution is
therefore a refinement on top of a capable agent, and removing it trades
precision for recall.

The ticket tests should be read the same way. Ticketed findings are more
likely than other findings to be genuine FP, and the agent repairs those
more often than chance, but they establish enrichment and not accuracy:
97 of the 665 findings the agent solved were real vulnerabilities
removed by mistake. The FN tickets show the same limit, since a pooled
61% of them point at a genuine miss. The contest step lets the agent
push back on a wrong verdict, as in the randbytes example of
§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 RQ2: Does the ticket mechanism behave as designed? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling"),
but it relies on a single critic. A natural next step is to separate the
judgments, for example with independent critics for FP and FN review
that must agree before a ticket is opened, to make this feedback more
reliable.

For a security team, the practical result is that the maintenance loop
can run without labels. A team with a new framework or a codebase no one
has labeled could point the agent at it and review the queries it
returns, instead of writing them. We tested this on a labeled benchmark
and a small pilot, so the claim is that the loop can work without
labels, not that it has been shown to work on unlabeled production code.

Two properties of the output matter for that use. First, the cost is
paid once and not on every scan. A run consumes substantial model tokens
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Agent Behaviour ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
but the suite it returns is ordinary code with no model dependency, so
scanning afterwards is as cheap as running any Joern query set, unlike
approaches that call a model on every repository and every run. Second,
the suite can be reviewed. The agent often records why a flagged case is
safe in an inline comment
(§[3](#S3 "3 Illustrative Example ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
so an engineer can audit a change, keep it, or revert it, which keeps a
person in the loop without asking them to write the rule.

The agent’s only memory across generations is a flat, read-only archive
of earlier suites. Structured memory \[[53](#bib.bib50),
[10](#bib.bib51)\] could let it reuse what it has learned instead of
re-deriving it after each repair. Replacing the stronger critic with the
agent’s own model would also show how much of the signal comes from the
critic’s prior knowledge.

## 8 Threats to Validity

We organize the threats along four axes, and for each we point to the
evidence in
§[5](#S5 "5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
that bounds it.

Internal validity. The agent explores the corpus directly, so some of
its gains may come from its own reading of the code and not from the
critic’s signal. The S2 ablation bounds this, since it keeps the agent’s
tools and corpus and removes only the critic, and it lands within S1’s
spread on $`F_{1}`$, so the outcome data cannot separate the two. The
critic is also a stronger model than the agent it supervises
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Models ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
so some of what we attribute to pseudo-labeling could be the critic’s
own prior knowledge leaking through its judgments. Isolating that
requires a same-model agent and critic, a local-context-only critic, and
a category-blind critic, which we have not run at the cost
§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Agent Behaviour ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
reports. For the real-world pilot, the ground truth is the introducing
commit found by SZZ attribution, which attributes lines to their last
modification and can misplace the true introduction.

External validity. We evaluate one language (Python) and one model pair,
and the OWASP benchmark is synthetic, so we do not claim the results
carry to other languages, model families, or real-world development. The
real-world pilot offers some evidence for transfer to organically
written code, but it covers 12 projects and 19 CVEs. Joern’s CPG
construction is bound by available RAM, so scaling to large repositories
or other program representations is open, and a single S1 run already
consumes a substantial number of Claude Sonnet 5 tokens
(§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 Agent Behaviour ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).
We did not study other budgets, so we cannot say how detector quality or
cost scale with a smaller or larger one.

Construct validity. The pseudo-labeled fitness is a proxy for the
ground-truth $`F_{1}`$ we cannot observe during search, and its two
halves are each imperfect. “Label-free” means the agent never sees which
files are vulnerable, not that the corpus offers no prior structure. The
target taxonomy $`T`$ is fixed (for OWASP, the benchmark’s own CWE (CWE)
categories), and Joern’s CPG exposes taint-relevant primitives that
narrow what a plausible query can look like. Both models were also
pretrained on public code and vulnerability discussion that may include
the OWASP style, and we did not test the critic under
semantic-preserving transformations that remove those cues. Some
reported accuracy may therefore reflect benchmark recognition and not
general detection ability. Agent and critic also come from one model
family, which may make the critic favor output that resembles its own
\[[43](#bib.bib63)\]. Youden’s $`J`$ for the evolved detector uses an
approximation of TN that upper-bounds it, so it is not on equal footing
with the baselines’ $`J`$. The evidence therefore supports a narrower
claim than “without labels.” The agent has no access to the withheld
answer key, on a benchmark whose taxonomy and surface patterns are not
entirely unfamiliar to the search.

Conclusion validity. The loop is stochastic, and ground-truth $`F_{1}`$
varies across independent runs
(§[5.1](#S5.SS1 "5.1 RQ1: Can static-analysis queries evolve without ground-truth labels, from scratch? ‣ 5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")),
with the charted run sitting above the mean. Each ablation has five
seeds, which bounds the aggregate metric and does not show the
mechanisms are inert, and a conventionally powered campaign would need
roughly ten times as many, which is why we add a Bayesian effect-size
estimate. The ablation tests are not corrected for multiplicity, and
$`F_{1}`$ is the single primary metric. The ticket tests are significant
across all 8 seeds, but they come from one benchmark and one model pair,
so they establish that the critic tracks ground truth in this setting
and not in general.

## 9 Conclusion

We asked whether a static-analysis rule set can evolve and repair itself
without ground-truth labels, the way a security engineer revises a set
of queries after spotting what it missed. Our results support three
findings, with the limits stated below. First, an agent can write
competitive queries from scratch. They reach a mean $`F_{1}`$ of
$`0.742{}`$ on the OWASP Benchmark for Python, ahead of five widely used
tools’ default configurations and in the same range as CodeQL once tuned
with the labels SESAA never gets. Second, the critic’s pseudo-labels
carry a real but imperfect signal. Its tickets are enriched for FP and
the agent’s repairs track them above chance, although some repairs
remove real vulnerabilities. Removing the critic or either ticket type
lowers the mean $`F_{1}`$ in the direction the design predicts. Third,
an agent reasoning over clean code can write rules that catch later
vulnerabilities. Queries evolved on clean code alone caught 10 of 19
vulnerabilities at the moment they were introduced. We hope these
findings help reframe the security scanner from a static tool into a
system that keeps itself current as the code it watches keeps changing.

## Appendix A Agent Tools

Each generational agent is a ReAct loop equipped with the six tools
below (seven when the FP-ticket mechanism is enabled,
§[2.1](#S2.SS1 "2.1 Pseudo-Labeled Fitness ‣ 2 System Architecture ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling"))
and no other side-effecting capabilities. In particular, bash executes
inside the sandboxed Docker analysis container, where /repo is the
agent’s mutable workspace and /corpus is the read-only OWASP corpus, and
is blocked from reading the withheld ground-truth labels or the critic
implementation.

think(reasoning)  
A reasoning checkpoint with no side effects. The agent records its plan
(which false negatives to target, what mutation to attempt) before
acting; this keeps the trajectory focused but does not alter any state.

bash(command)  
Runs a shell command in the analysis container. Used to explore the
corpus, grep for patterns, and write detector files (.sc queries or .py
tools) via here-documents. Commands that reference the ground-truth
directory or critic files are rejected, as is sleep.

analyse_corpus()  
Compiles and runs all custom detectors over the full corpus ($`\sim`$2
min) and returns a per-query findings summary together with the critic’s
qualitative feedback (coverage gaps, false-positive patterns). It
measures the current suite but does not commit it or end the generation.
The agent may call it repeatedly, revising detectors between calls,
before deciding the suite is ready
(§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Evolution Configuration ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")).

submit()  
Commits the current suite as this generation’s candidate and ends the
agent’s turn, so each generation yields exactly one committed candidate
(§[5](#S5 "5 Results ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling"))
regardless of how many times analyse_corpus() was called beforehand.

delete_query(name)  
Removes a detector file the agent previously wrote. Because a single
non-compiling query makes analyse_corpus() fail for _all_ queries,
deleting an unfixable one unblocks the rest.

inspect_prior_candidates(candidate_id)  
Read-only access to the archive of past candidates and their critic
evaluations (reasoning, coverage gaps, false-positive patterns), giving
the agent non-Markovian memory across generations. Called with no
argument it lists all candidates; with an ID it returns that candidate’s
full critic evaluation.

## Appendix B Prompts

We reproduce verbatim the four prompts that define the system’s
behaviour: the three agent-facing prompts (system, per-generation, and
the critic feedback injected back into the agent), plus the critic’s
precision-judge prompt that computes the precision half of the fitness
signal. Template variables (e.g. {gen}, {parent_id}) are filled at
runtime.

### B.1 System Prompt

The system prompt establishes the agent’s role, workspace layout,
available tools, and the measure/refine/commit loop;
§[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Evolution Configuration ‣ 4 Methodology ‣ Self-Evolving Static Analysis via LLM Pseudo-Labeling")
describes the same mechanism in prose.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

1 You are a security researcher tasked with evolving

2 vulnerability detectors for Joern. Joern uses Code Property

3 Graphs (CPG) to analyze codebases and find security

4 vulnerabilities. You will see a corpus of Python code in

5 {CORPUS_PATH}.

6

7 analyse_corpus() returns a compact summary (findings per

8 query) and writes detailed critic feedback to

9 ‘/repo/analysis_details.json‘. Read that file for the

10 critic’s qualitative assessment (coverage gaps, FP

11 patterns). Maximize real detections (true positives) while

12 minimizing false positives.

13

14 \## Your objective

15 The only thing measured is detector quality. Run

16 ‘analyse_corpus()‘ to see how your detectors perform on the

17 corpus; when the results improve, call ‘submit(desc="...")‘

18 to commit a new candidate and end your turn. That feedback

19 loop is the whole game -- your detectors are the deliverable.

20 Queries must be written in Joern’s Scala-based query

21 language (‘.sc‘ files); Python detector tools are also

22 allowed.

23

24 ‘analyse_corpus()‘ is a pure measurement step -- call it as

25 often as you like to test and refine; it does NOT commit.

26 The committed candidate persists to the next generation, so

27 iterate (analyse, read errors/critic, fix, re-analyse)

28 before you submit.

29

30 \## How you get there is up to you

31 You’re free to write whatever helps you do that well --

32 exploratory scripts, helper tools, notes, scratch files,

33 documentation -- anywhere under /repo. Nothing below is

34 mandatory ritual; they are aids that tend to pay off:

35 - Read /repo/NOTES.md -- your persistent lab notebook from

36 prior generations (detectors that already work and

37 shouldn’t be broken, FP-prone patterns, ideas to try).

38 Build on it instead of starting cold.

39 - Explore the corpus and skim /repo/docs/ before writing a

40 detector, so your query matches patterns that are

41 actually present.

42 - Jot down what each analyse_corpus() run taught you in

43 NOTES.md while it’s fresh -- which query files yield real

44 true positives, which patterns were FP-prone, what to try

45 next -- so the next generation inherits it.

46

47 Do these if they help; skip them if they don’t. Spend your

48 effort where it moves detector quality.

49

50 \## Environment

51 Your working directory is ‘/repo‘ with your mutable

52 detector code:

53 - ‘/repo/joern_analyser/‘ -- your working copy (changes

54 here are evolved)

55 - ‘/repo/docs/‘ -- documentation for reference

56 - ‘/corpus/‘ -- read-only analysis corpus

57

58 \## Available Tools

59 - ‘think()‘ -- reason through your approach

60 - ‘bash(command="...")‘ -- run shell commands in the

61 container (write files, explore, grep). ‘/repo/‘ is your

62 workspace, ‘/corpus/‘ is the corpus

63 - ‘delete_query(name="X.sc")‘ -- delete a detector you

64 wrote (use to remove a query that won’t compile)

65 - ‘analyse_corpus()‘ -- run detectors on corpus and

66 measure quality (expensive, ~2 min); returns

67 findings-per-query counts and critic feedback.

68 Repeatable -- does NOT commit. Call it freely to test

69 and iterate.

70 - ‘submit(desc="...")‘ -- commit the current detectors as

71 a new generation and end your turn. Runs a fresh

72 analysis, archives the candidate with its score, then

73 ends the generation. Call this only when you are

74 satisfied; you cannot edit afterwards.

75 - ‘ticket(action, id, note)‘ -- inspect and act on FP

76 (false-positive) tickets the critic opens in

77 /repo/tickets/. ‘ticket(action="list")‘ shows open

78 tickets; ‘ticket(action="show", id=...)‘ prints one. To

79 clear a ticket that really is a false positive, tighten

80 its named query so it stops firing, then re-run

81 analyse_corpus(). If you believe the finding is a REAL

82 vulnerability, ‘ticket(action="dismiss", id=...,

83 note="why it’s real")‘ -- the critic re-judges with your

84 argument and only closes the ticket if convinced

85 (limited attempts)."
