### B.2 Generation Prompt

Each generation receives this prompt, which defines the fitness
function, scoring insights, valid vulnerability types, the parent
workspace, and the detector-writing workflow with syntax constraints.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

1 \## Generation {gen} of {total}

2

3 MESSAGE BUDGET: {max_messages} messages. Focus.

4

5 {universe_line}Workspace: branched from {parent_id}

6

7 \## Goal: Maximize Fitness

8

9 Fitness = sqrt(precision x type_coverage)

10

11 Where:

12 - Precision = mean of per-group precision scores. Each

13 query group (findings from one .sc file) is independently

14 judged by an LLM that samples a few findings and decides

15 if they are real vulnerabilities.

16 - Type coverage = fraction of the target vulnerability

17 classes that your detectors actually exercise (emit at

18 least one finding for). This is a density-independent

19 recall proxy -- covering MORE distinct vulnerability

20 classes raises it, regardless of how many files each

21 fires on.

22

23 \### Key Scoring Insights

24 - Both precision AND type coverage must be strong. A

25 firehose that sprays one class across every file but is

26 mostly FP scores poorly (low precision). A perfect

27 detector that only covers 1 vulnerability class also

28 scores poorly (low coverage).

29 - Groups are evaluated independently. A group scoring 0.0

30 drags down mean precision.

31 - Better to have 3 groups at precision=1.0 covering 3

32 different vulnerability classes than 5 groups, all of the

33 same class, where 2 score 0.0.

34 - The judge samples ~5-8 findings per group. Very small

35 groups (\<5 findings) are judged in full.

36 - Type coverage rewards detecting MANY DISTINCT

37 vulnerability classes, not many files. To raise it, add

38 detectors for classes that currently produce no findings

39 -- spraying more findings of a class you already cover

40 does not help coverage.

41 - If findings haven’t changed between runs, scores are

42 cached (deterministic). Only new/changed findings get

43 re-judged.

44

45 \## Valid Vulnerability Types

46

47 Your query filename MUST use one of these types as prefix

48 (e.g., ‘SQL_INJECTION\_\_HIGH\_\_desc.sc‘).

49 Findings with unrecognized types are classified as UNKNOWN

50 and automatically score precision=0.0:

51

52 SQL_INJECTION, COMMAND_INJECTION, XSS, PATH_TRAVERSAL,

53 CODE_INJECTION, LDAP_INJECTION, XXE, DESERIALIZATION,

54 SSTI, IDOR, BROKEN_ACCESS_CONTROL,

55 BROKEN_AUTHENTICATION, INFORMATION_DISCLOSURE,

56 CRLF_INJECTION, LOG_INJECTION, SSRF,

57 WEAK_CRYPTOGRAPHY, WEAK_ENTROPY, WEAK_RANDOMNESS,

58 XPATH_INJECTION, INSECURE_COOKIE, OPEN_REDIRECT,

59 SESSION_FIXATION, TRUST_BOUNDARY_VIOLATION

60

61 \## Current State

62 {metrics_display}

63

64 \## Writing Detectors

65

66 CRITICAL: Only write a detector if you understand taint

67 analysis. Do NOT write bare ‘cpg.call().l.foreach‘

68 queries -- they don’t find real vulnerabilities. Use

69 ‘reachableByFlows(SOURCE_PATTERNS)‘ for taint tracking.

70

71 Steps:

72

73 1. Analyze corpus samples to identify:

74 - What sink functions should be detected?

75 - What argument positions contain user input?

76 - What taint sources are relevant? (request

77 parameters, uploaded files, etc.)

78 - What vulnerability name to use?

79

80 2. Write a taint-tracking query. Example (SQL Injection):

81 cpg.call("execute\|executeQuery\|executeUpdate")

82 .argument(0)

83 .reachableByFlows(

84 cpg.method.name(".\*request.\*\|.\*getParam.\*")

85 .parameter)

86 .l

87 .foreach { node =\>

88 val lineNum = node.lineNumber

89 .getOrElse(-1).toString

90 println(s"\${node.file}\|\|\|\${lineNum}\|\|\|"

91 + s"SQL Injection\|\|\|\${node.code}")

92 }

93 - Write to /repo/joern_analyser/analyses/custom/

94 queries/TYPE\_\_SEVERITY\_\_description.sc

95 - Use bash heredocs: bash(command="cat \>

96 /repo/.../X.sc \<\< ’EOF’\n...\nEOF")

97 - Use single-quoted EOF delimiter to avoid shell

98 interpolation of \$ in Scala

99

100 3. Analyze with analyse_corpus() to evaluate fitness

101

102 \## Workflow (MANDATORY - FOLLOW IN THIS ORDER)

103

104 PHASE 0: READ DOCUMENTATION FIRST

105 - docs/fundamentals/cpg.md -- understand Code Property

106 Graph

107 - docs/query-language/cpgql-reference.md -- how to write

108 queries

109 - docs/detectors/sql-injection.md -- example detector

110 patterns

111 - KEY RULE: DO NOT include ‘importCpg‘ in your query --

112 framework adds it

113 - Check existing detectors (bash grep) to see working

114 patterns

115

116 \### CRITICAL: Scala/CPGQL Syntax Errors to Avoid

117

118 DO NOT use ‘reachableBy(sources:\_\*)‘ -- this DOES NOT

119 COMPILE in Joern 4.x.

120

121 The ‘:\_\*‘ splat annotation is invalid for

122 ‘reachableBy‘/‘reachableByFlows‘ parameters.

123

124 WRONG (will fail with "Sequence argument type annotation

125 ‘\*‘ cannot be used here"):

126 val sources = cpg.method.name(".\*param.\*").parameter

127 cpg.call("exec").argument(0)

128 .filter(c =\> c.argument

129 .reachableBy(sources:\_\*).nonEmpty)

130

131 CORRECT -- pass the traversal directly:

132 cpg.call("exec").argument(0)

133 .reachableByFlows(

134 cpg.method.name(".\*param.\*").parameter)

135 .l

136 .foreach { flow =\> ... }

137

138 Always use the ‘reachableByFlows‘ taint-tracking pattern

139 -- do NOT invent new taint-tracking patterns or write

140 bare ‘cpg.call‘ queries.

141

142 PHASE 1: EXPLORE CORPUS (now that you understand Joern)

143 {corpus_hint}

144

145 Read actual files from the corpus. Grep for patterns.

146 Identify what vulnerabilities are actually present.

147

148 PHASE 2: IMPLEMENT WITH JOERN (only after understanding

149 Joern + corpus)

150 Design and implement detectors using proper Scala/CPGQL

151 syntax from the docs.

152 Test with analyse_corpus() -- each run automatically

153 commits the current state as a new generation and seeds

154 the next.

### B.3 Critic Feedback Template

After each evaluation, the critic returns a structured summary injected
into the agent’s context to guide the next mutation.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

1 ESTIMATED PRECISION: {precision:.2%}

2 ({tp_verified} of {total_findings} sampled findings

3 verified genuine)

4 COVERAGE SCORE: {coverage:.2%}

5 (detector found patterns in ~{coverage_pct}% of

6 sampled files)

7 CRITIC FITNESS: {fitness:.2%}

8 (goal: approach 1.0)

Listing 3: Critic feedback template (verbatim).

### B.4 Critic Precision Judge

The precision half of the fitness signal is produced by an LLM judge.
For each detector group (the findings emitted by one .sc query), the
critic samples a few representative findings spanning distinct files and
asks the model to count how many are genuinely exploitable; the group’s
precision is the fraction judged real, and overall precision is the mean
across groups. Sampling scales with group size (all findings if
$`\leq 5`$, up to $`8`$ for medium groups, $`5`$ for large groups), and
unchanged findings are cached to keep scoring deterministic across runs.

[⬇](data:text/plain;base64,)

1 You are a security expert. Below are {n_sampled}

2 representative findings from a group of {n_total}

3 detector findings of type {vuln_type}.

4 For EACH, decide if it is a REAL exploitable

5 vulnerability (not just a code smell or theoretical

6 concern). Be strict: a finding is real only if

7 untrusted input can reach a dangerous sink without

8 proper sanitization.

9

10 {findings_json}

11

12 Respond with JSON:

13 {"real_count": \<int 0-{n_sampled}\>, "reason": "..."}

Listing 4: Critic precision-judge prompt (verbatim; {n_sampled},
{n_total}, {vuln_type}, and {findings_json} are filled per group at
runtime).
